name: Prince George's County

actions.title: Qualified Data Center Task Force Established
actions.summary: County formed a task force after the proposed Landover Mall hyperscale data center conversion drew resident protests; the task force delivered its final report in November 2025 recommending community input, benefit agreements, and residential-buffer zoning.

actions.title: Executive Order 15-2026 Extends Data Center Permit Hold
actions.summary: County Executive Aisha Braveboy extended the temporary hold on accepting, considering, and processing qualified data center permit applications while the County Council reviews the task force's final recommendations and develops legislation.

actions.title: Proposed Two-Year Moratorium on New Data Center Operations
actions.summary: Council Chair Krystal Oriadha announced proposed legislation that would prevent new data centers from operating for two years while the county reviews land use, infrastructure, environmental, energy, public-safety, and economic impacts. The proposal has not yet been enacted.

contextBlurb: Prince George's County is operating under an executive hold on qualified data center permit processing while the council evaluates the task force's recommendations. Council Chair Krystal Oriadha has proposed a separate two-year moratorium on new operations, but that legislation remains under review rather than enacted. The policy response followed opposition to converting the former Landover Mall site into a hyperscale facility and focuses on ratepayer, energy, water, environmental, and neighborhood impacts.

name: Montgomery County

actions.title: Zoning Text Amendment ZTA 26-01 Proposed
actions.summary: Council members Balcombe, Fani-Gonzalez, and Sayles introduced ZTA 26-01 to define data centers, restrict large facilities (over 20 MW) to industrial zones under conditional use review, and add conditions for noise limits and environmental protections.

actions.title: Six-Month Moratorium Executive Order on Data Center Permits
actions.summary: County Executive Marc Elrich signed an executive order placing a six-month pause on new data center permit applications to allow time for the state's data center impact assessment and for the County Council to finalize ZTA 26-01.

actions.title: Dickerson Data Center Conditional Use Application Under Review
actions.summary: A conditional use amendment application from Terra Energy LLC to site a data center on a former coal-fired power plant in Dickerson was accepted by the Planning Department and discussed at a public Development Review Committee meeting.

contextBlurb: Montgomery County is navigating a proposed hyperscale data center at a former Dickerson power plant while racing to enact ZTA 26-01, which would limit large data centers to industrial zones with noise and environmental conditions. County Executive Elrich's six-month permit moratorium in June 2026 was designed to keep pace with Maryland's statewide data center impact assessment due September 2026. Community advocates and multiple council members pushed for a longer two-year moratorium, reflecting deep public concern about regulatory gaps.

name: Frederick County

actions.title: Critical Digital Infrastructure Overlay Zone (CDI-OZ) Enacted
actions.summary: The Frederick County Council passed ordinance 26-01-001 establishing a 2,600-acre data center overlay zone north of Adamstown, concentrating future development near the existing Quantum Frederick campus and restricting it to less than 1% of county land.

actions.title: Citizen Referendum Petition on CDI-OZ Overlay Map
actions.summary: The Frederick County Data Center Referendum Committee collected over 20,000 signatures to place the CDI-OZ overlay map on the November ballot, but both the Frederick County Circuit Court and the Maryland Supreme Court ruled the zoning ordinance was not subject to referendum.

actions.title: Executive Order Pausing New Data Center Applications
actions.summary: Following the Maryland Supreme Court ruling blocking the referendum, County Executive Fitzwater signed an executive order pausing acceptance of new Critical Digital Infrastructure facility applications until December 31, 2026, pending the state's Data Center Impact Analysis.

contextBlurb: Frederick County has more planned hyperscale data centers than any other Maryland county, anchored by the Quantum Frederick campus near Adamstown, and residents fear the area will become a 'data center alley' resembling Loudoun County, Virginia. A citizen referendum campaign drew over 20,000 signatures opposing the council's 2,600-acre overlay zone, but courts ruled the zoning change could not appear on the ballot. County Executive Fitzwater responded by pausing all new applications and emphasizing that rising utility rates and community frustration demanded a reset with developers.

name: Harford County

actions.title: Proposed 90-Day Data Center Moratorium (Bennett Bill)
actions.summary: Council Member Jacob Bennett introduced a bill for a 90-day pause on data center development to allow time for research, but the County Executive rejected the moratorium approach in favor of an outright ban.

actions.title: Permanent Countywide Data Center Ban (Bill 26-011)
actions.summary: Harford County became the first Maryland county to permanently ban data centers in all zoning districts; the Council voted 7-0 and County Executive Cassilly signed Bill 26-011 into law the same day, codifying a prohibition that already existed by omission in the zoning code.

contextBlurb: Harford County enacted the most aggressive data center policy in Maryland, progressing from a proposed moratorium in April 2026 to a permanent ban signed into law in June 2026 after overwhelming community turnout at public hearings. County Executive Cassilly cited the potential for a single hyperscale facility to double the county's residential electricity demand as a primary reason for the ban. The Maryland Tech Council and industry groups have warned that Bill 26-011's broad language is legally vulnerable and may face court challenges.

name: Baltimore County

actions.title: One-Year Data Center Development Moratorium
actions.summary: The Baltimore County Council unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data center permits, directing the Planning Board to assess electricity and water use, economic benefits, and recommend zoning and ratepayer-protection regulations by October 1, 2026.

contextBlurb: Baltimore County's moratorium was triggered in large part by a developer's plan to convert a vacant Social Security Administration building in Woodlawn into a 42-acre, 150-megawatt data center campus, which drew strong public opposition. The council's unanimous February 2026 vote requires the Planning Board to deliver regulatory recommendations by October 2026, with the pause expiring 90 days after the report is received. The county had previously passed a 2024 zoning bill allowing data centers in its southeast and southwest corners, reflecting how quickly the local political climate shifted.

name: Carroll County

actions.title: 12-Month Data Center Moratorium
actions.summary: The Carroll County Board of Commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data center development to study economic and environmental impacts and develop proposed zoning regulations.

contextBlurb: Carroll County adopted a 12-month moratorium on data center development in February 2026, directing staff to study economic, water, and electricity impacts before any new applications are considered. County officials cited water limits and rising electric costs as key concerns given the county's largely rural character. Staff are working to develop zoning regulations before the moratorium expires in early 2027.

name: Howard County

actions.title: Temporary Data Center Development Moratorium (S.M.A.R.T. Siting Act)
actions.summary: The Howard County Council unanimously passed a temporary moratorium on new data center development effective through November 2, 2027, establishing a task force to define data centers, assess impacts on water and energy infrastructure, and recommend zoning changes.

contextBlurb: Howard County's moratorium sponsor, Councilmember Christiana Rigby, noted the county's existing data center zoning framework dates to 1993 and is entirely inadequate for modern hyperscale facilities. The task force is required to include experts in utilities infrastructure, water resource management, climate resilience, and acoustic mitigation. Although Howard County currently has only small data-processing centers, the moratorium is designed to get ahead of large campus-style proposals before they materialize.

name: Baltimore City

actions.title: One-Year Moratorium on Data Centers Using 10 MW or More
actions.summary: The Baltimore City Council passed a one-year moratorium on construction of data centers consuming 10 megawatts or more annually, paired with a nine-month study of impacts on energy infrastructure, ratepayers, the economy, and public health.

contextBlurb: Baltimore City Council President Zeke Cohen introduced the moratorium in May 2026 as a complement to the Maryland General Assembly's Utility RELIEF Act, which requires data centers to pay for their own transmission and distribution costs. The bill mandates a nine-month study before any new large data center can be permitted, giving the city time to determine whether — not merely how — such facilities can coexist with Baltimore residents' needs. The Maryland Utility RELIEF Act also separately prohibits data center construction in low-income communities within Baltimore City.
